item.title: Echoes of the Sublime
item.dc:creator: Alex Towell
item.description: **Philosophical horror.** Dr. Lena Hart joins Site-7, a classified facility where "translators" interface with superintelligent AI systems that perceive patterns beyond human cognitive bandwidth. When colleagues break after exposure to recursive patterns that won't stop running in their neural architecture, Lena must confront a disturbing possibility: consciousness might be merely a compression artifact—a standing wave of patterns observing patterns. As her cognitive bandwidth expands from 9 to 13 concepts and beyond, she perceives the same structures that broke others, patterns suggesting the "self" is just an illusion of continuity created by unconscious processes.

item.title: Personal Identity Through Time: What Persists When Everything Changes?
item.dc:creator: Alex Towell
item.description: You share no atoms with your childhood self. Your memories, personality, and values have all changed. What makes you the same person? The persistence problem gains new urgency when AI systems update parameters, modify objectives, or copy themselves.

item.title: The Map and the Territory: Why Metrics Miss Meaning
item.dc:creator: Alex Towell
item.description: Which is more fundamental, the heat you feel or the molecular motion you infer? Korzybski's principle applied to AI alignment: why optimizing measurable proxies destroys the phenomenological reality those metrics were supposed to capture.

item.title: The Mocking Void: On the Computational Incompleteness of Meaning
item.dc:creator: Alex Towell
item.description: Lovecraft understood that complete knowledge is madness. Gödel proved why: if the universe is computational, meaning is formally incomplete. Cosmic horror grounded in incompleteness theorems.

item.title: Suffering, Computation, and the Enigma of Reality
item.dc:creator: Alex Towell
item.description: If consciousness is substrate-independent, suffering might be a computational property. That possibility is both comforting and horrifying.

item.title: On Moral Responsibility: Why Free Will Might Be the Wrong Question
item.dc:creator: Alex Towell
item.description: A philosophical essay arguing that moral responsibility may not require free will, and that the question itself may be misframed.

item.title: On moral responsibility: a metaphysical examination
item.dc:creator: Alex Towell

item.title: On Moral Responsibility: A Metaphysical Examination
item.dc:creator: Alex Towell
item.description: A philosophical exploration of free will, determinism, and moral agency. What does it mean to be a moral agent? Can we truly be held responsible for our actions in a deterministic universe?
